items.text: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI. On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic. items.title: "I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people are using
items.text: "I'm not at a point where I trust the agent, especially with stuff that people are using." From Micky (@Rasmic), who's taught 100K+ people to build with AI: "The manual review is like the final step. All the work's done, and I have as much evidence from the agent as possible. With evidence-driven testing, before and after, and even greploop, we're trying to build trust. The agent presents evidence: This is the work that's done, and this is why it's good. For anyone who's been a developer for any time, manual review is probably the worst part of your job. This sort of helps minimize the friction." 📌 Watch Micky's full 4-step workflow here: https://t.co/ju9aMQKaCE

items.title: Day 7/ We have increased default context length for GPT-6
items.text: Day 7/ We have increased default context length for GPT-6.1 Sol to 500k when used through Codex & Work, up from 272k or an ~ 80% increase. We will go higher in the future, but it helps reduce occurrence of compactions and with tasks that require keeping a lot of context and nuance over periods of time. It was carefully tested and is the new sweet spot for most of our users. You can still override it if you want to be higher our lower, with maximum context length of GPT-6.1 Sol of 1M.

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is...
items.text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For...

items.title: Frontier Chips for Frontier AI Labs, with Walter Goodwin, Founder/CEO of Fractile
items.text: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:30 Right now, we're trying to build a single chip. If you crack open an NVIDIA system, it has anywhere between kind of six and nine custom chips all built by NVIDIA to come together to build something that is really, really potent. So there's already a gap there. You know, it'd be great to be productive enough that we could start to build our own responses in that same kind of way. This idea of being able to have at any given moment a kind of rolling frontier of bets that you hope are deeply aligned in which you're ready to trigger the ramp of, this is a huge advantage if you can kind of build that machine and build that engine.
